transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-21
Time: 3:34 PM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Miguel Santos (Redwood ML Eng), Rachel Kim (Polaris Head of ML), Arun Patel (Polaris Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Polaris SRE), Evan Brooks (Polaris Research)
Shared artifacts: Polaris sample dataset (link), Redwood quantization bench sheet (https://redwood.internal/bench/polaris-qtz), slide deck (shared in chat)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: alright everyone thanks for joining, uh today is the deep dive on quantization implications for your models. Priya and Miguel will run through the runtime perf and we can talk ops and VPC afterwards.
[00:18] Rachel Kim: thanks Jordan. we're mainly concerned about accuracy regressions — we saw some delta in a quick INT8 run and want to understand tradeoffs.
[00:27] Priya Nair: yeah totally, so agenda: quick recap of model profile, then kernel/runtime behavior, batching and KV cache effects, then GPTQ/AWQ results we've seen on similar workloads, and finally next steps for a pilot.
[00:41] Arun Patel: quick note, we have strict networking — VPC peering only, no public egress from inference nodes, and HSM-managed keys for our customer data.
[00:50] Miguel Santos: got it, we'll cover VPC/on-prem considerations at the end.
[01:02] Priya Nair: model profile: you're running a 7b decoder-only transformer with long context up to 8k, many short queries (50-200 tokens) and some long summaries. Typical seq length on generation is 120 tokens. That pattern favors lower latency single-request performance over large throughput.
[01:28] Rachel Kim: yes that sounds right. our main worry is that quantization will push quality too far down for the summary jobs.
[01:36] Priya Nair: totally reasonable. quick note on quant families: INT8 (symmetric/asymmetric) gives strong memory reduction but often needs calibration and can introduce bias on some heads; FP8 gives smaller memory gains than INT8 but preserves FP semantics and often maintains accuracy better; GPTQ (post-training quant) is good for 3-4 bit but can be brittle depending on layerwise Hessian approximations; AWQ is newer — per-channel scaling plus AWE-type corrections that often give closer float fidelity at 3-4 bits.
[02:10] Evan Brooks: when you say brittle, do you mean different seeds/compilers lead to variance?
[02:14] Miguel Santos: yep, sometimes GPTQ's reconstruction error shows up only for certain prompt classes, we call that patchy regressions. AWQ tends to be more robust but trades some extra compute at runtime.
[02:28] Rachel Kim: patchy regressions are the worst because they break spot checks.
[02:32] Priya Nair: exactly. for Polaris' dataset our initial sims show GPTQ 4-bit had a -1.8 BLEU-style or rouge-ish delta on the abstractive subset; AWQ 4-bit was more like -0.6. INT8 (symmetric) had near zero delta but memory savings less dramatic depending on embedding mat shapes.
[02:56] Arun Patel: can you clarify cost/latency tradeoffs? if AWQ requires extra ops, do we lose our latency SLO?
[03:02] Priya Nair: good question. AWQ does a small per-kernel correction that adds ~2-6% wall time in our runtime on A100 for short seqs, but it helps avoid re-running the model or re-ranking. For batchy throughput workloads the overhead is amortized and often <2%.
[03:22] Jordan Lee: note: these numbers are from Redwood Hosted profiles; dedicated pools can have slight diffs depending on kernel build and driver.
[03:30] Sofia Alvarez: we run on-prem with mixed GPU types (A100 and a couple of T4s for burst); how does mixed hardware affect choices?
[03:38] Miguel Santos: mixed hardware complicates kernel selection. our runtime will pick kernels per-device; for the same model we may route smaller latency-sensitive requests to A100s and batch larger ones on T4s. With quantization, ensuring the same model weights across devices is key — use deterministic serialization (we have a tool to export quant artifacts).
[04:00] Rachel Kim: what's the story with KV cache and quant? we cache past keys heavily in our app.
[04:06] Priya Nair: KV cache is orthogonal — it's just tensors stored in GPU memory. Quantized model weights don't change kv cache format. But be mindful: lower precision affects per-token compute; if you're relying on large KV caches to reduce recomputation, quantization helps by shrinking model footprint and letting you hold longer contexts in GPU memory. We saw a customer move from 4k to 16k effective with AWQ 4-bit and a smaller batch footprint.
[04:36] Evan Brooks: any gotchas with prefix caching and FP8?
[04:40] Miguel Santos: you still keep KV cache in FP16/FP32 for stability; we do not quantize KV caches. So FP8/INT8 applies to weights; caches stay in higher precision.
[04:51] Jordan Lee: here's a quick run of numbers from our bench sheet for a similar 7b profile (short seqs): float16 P50 18ms, GPTQ-4 P50 12ms, AWQ-4 P50 13ms, INT8 P50 11ms. P95s have larger spreads though — GPTQ P95 sometimes spikes if recompile or fallback occurs.
[05:16] Rachel Kim: why would GPTQ cause spikes?
[05:20] Priya Nair: spikes often due to fallback paths — e.g., some ops not supported by the fast kernel for that quant layout so runtime reverts to a slower path. Also cached KV alignment and certain attention implementations can cause extra memcpy/format conversions.
[05:36] Arun Patel: is that something Redwood runtime can smooth out?
[05:40] Miguel Santos: we have logging and kernel-selection heuristics; for dedicated pools we can precompile the right kernels and avoid runtime fallback. For Hosted/AWS/GCP multi-tenant it's trickier but still manageable with pinned instances.
[05:55] Jordan Lee: quick interruption — anyone seeing audio issues? no? ok.
[06:00] Priya Nair: moving on to batching: for your mix of many small requests we recommend smart batching with max-latency budget of 50ms and dynamic batching up to 8 requests to preserve P95. Continuous batching helps but configuration matters.
[06:16] Rachel Kim: what about batching + KV cache? does batching force cache flushes?
[06:19] Miguel Santos: no, batching is orthogonal — KV cache is per-session. When we batch multiple sessions we gather the current prefix lengths, pad, and concat. The runtime keeps separate KV slices. The main overhead is padding cost; quant helps by reducing per-token compute so batch windows can be slightly larger without hurting latency.
[06:40] Evan Brooks: curious about FP8 — is Redwood supporting FP8 kernels?
[06:44] Priya Nair: yes we support FP8 on newer GPUs with the right driver and compiler flags, but adoption is less mature. FP8 can give very close float behaviour with smaller memory, but some ops have numerical instability on certain activation ranges — we've seen that with very aggressive context lengths.
[07:02] Rachel Kim: any examples where FP8 would be preferable to AWQ/GPTQ?
[07:06] Miguel Santos: FP8 is good when you want minimal code changes and hardware native support, and when your accuracy metrics are super sensitive to 1:1 float semantics. AWQ/GPTQ are more aggressive size tradeoffs. FP8 wins on stability, AWQ wins on size+accuracy, GPTQ wins on raw size but needs careful validation.
[07:26] Jordan Lee: for Polaris' case given you want long contexts and high fidelity on summaries, we're leaning toward AWQ-4 as a first candidate — it reduces memory similar to GPTQ but with fewer regressions.
[07:38] Rachel Kim: okay that's promising. can you show example evals?
[07:42] Priya Nair: yes — I pulled a quick eval in the shared bench sheet: three sample prompts from your abstractive set, float16 outputs vs GPTQ4 vs AWQ4. For prompt A GPTQ had hallucinated a date, AWQ matched float; for prompt B GPTQ shortened a clause. This is the patchy regression behavior.
[08:03] Evan Brooks: is this dataset-specific?
[08:05] Priya Nair: very much so — that's why we recommended running models on your real validation corpus.
[08:10] Arun Patel: about benchmarking: do you need perf access to our infra or can you run synthetic tests?
[08:15] Miguel Santos: both. we can run synthetic microbenchmarks on Redwood infra to get kernel-level numbers, but we need your validation set for accuracy regressions. For latency P95 on your cluster we'd prefer to run a short pilot on dedicated nodes or have you run our bench container and upload traces.
[08:32] Rachel Kim: we can probably spin up a small pool for a week. peering constraints apply.
[08:35] Jordan Lee: great. on security: we support VPC peering and private deployment, and for on-prem we ship an air-gapped bundle. We'll need firewall rules and SSH keys or an S3 endpoint for artifact exchange.
[08:49] Sofia Alvarez: we use HSM for keys, do you integrate with external KMS/HSM?
[08:53] Priya Nair: yes we support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, YubiHSM common patterns). For private deployments we can point to your in-cluster KMS.
[09:02] Evan Brooks: any non-obvious perf regressions when using HSM?
[09:06] Miguel Santos: HSM is used for key unwrap at startup; operationally negligible during inference. The main perf constraints are network egress and storage I/O for large KV caches if you use networked volumes.
[09:18] Rachel Kim: re: accuracy metrics — we use ROUGE-L and an internal factuality score. What thresholds should we set for a pilot?
[09:26] Jordan Lee: typical customers accept up to ~1% absolute drop on ROUGE-L for 4-bit if latency/cost gains offset it; but that depends on business tolerance. For Polaris I'd recommend a strict threshold of 0.5% and manual spot checks for hallucination patterns.
[09:43] Priya Nair: we'll add those thresholds into the evaluation harness and flag any prompts with >0.5% delta. Also run targeted checks for hallucination class.
[09:52] Arun Patel: can we see the end-to-end cost impact? like tokens per second and dollar delta for dedicated vs hosted?
[09:58] Jordan Lee: we can provide a modelled delta. ballpark: AWQ-4 on A100 reduces token cost ~2.5-3x vs float16 when accounting for memory savings and packing; GPTQ4 can be 3.5x but with higher risk; INT8 depends on sparsity and layer shapes. We'll run an exact calc for your request pattern.
[10:19] Evan Brooks: what about FP8 on T4s?
[10:22] Miguel Santos: T4 doesn't have FP8 hardware support, so FP8 emulation is slow. T4 is good for INT8/quantized kernels though.
[10:30] Rachel Kim: earlier you mentioned kernel fallbacks causing P95 spikes. how do you prevent that in dedicated pools?
[10:35] Priya Nair: in dedicated we prebuild kernels for your model, pin compatible driver versions, and run a warmup suite to trigger all code paths. That way the runtime doesn't JIT/compile during live traffic.
[10:47] Sofia Alvarez: would that be part of a pilot?
[10:49] Jordan Lee: yes, pilot includes a kernel warmup run and a short validation window.
[10:54] Priya Nair: quick aside on reproducibility: GPTQ artifacts can be nondeterministic unless you fix the RNG/compilation flags. We recommend generating artifacts in a controlled env — we can help with a reproducible docker image.
[11:08] Rachel Kim: good to know.
[11:11] Jordan Lee: are there any vendor lock-in concerns with AWQ/GPTQ formats?
[11:14] Miguel Santos: formats vary. GPTQ artifacts are common and many toolkits support them; AWQ is emerging — we provide exporter/importer tools. Redwood's runtime supports multiple quant backends to reduce lock-in.
[11:27] Evan Brooks: ok from infra perspective we need the steps to set up peering and a small test cluster.
[11:31] Arun Patel: noted.
[11:33] Priya Nair: going to show a short microbenchmark excerpt (read from bench sheet) — this is synthetic: float16 12.1k tokens/s, GPTQ4 34.8k tokens/s, AWQ4 30.2k tokens/s on A100, with P95 spikes for GPTQ in 5% of runs. These map to the P50 times I mentioned earlier.
[11:55] Rachel Kim: do you have failure modes logged in the sheet? would like examples.
[11:59] Priya Nair: yes, the sheet has a notes column — e.g., prompt family B triggered an attention collapse with GPTQ where a token bleeds earlier. We'll annotate and share.
[12:10] Jordan Lee: ok let's cover pilot scope and timeline. we propose: week 1 — artifact exchange + kernel warmup; week 2 — run GPTQ vs AWQ full eval on your validation set; week 3 — analyze results and pick config; week 4 — pilot on dedicated pool for 1 week with SLO monitoring. Does that align?
[12:29] Rachel Kim: sounds reasonable. can we compress to three weeks?
[12:33] Jordan Lee: maybe, if Polaris provides infra access and artifacts immediately. Priya, Miguel — feasible?
[12:39] Miguel Santos: yes we can tighten weeks 1+2 into one if customer runs our bench container in their environment and shares logs.
[12:47] Arun Patel: we'll try to provision peered test nodes by Monday.
[12:50] Priya Nair: great. a couple more quick technical Q&A before we wrap.
[12:54] Evan Brooks: do you recommend re-ranking as a mitigation for small regressions?
[12:58] Priya Nair: absolutely — often we keep a small float16 reranker (or n-best rescoring) to catch hallucinations; that gives a good accuracy budget while still using quantized generator. Cost wise it's small because rerankers can run on CPU or cheaper GPU.
[13:14] Rachel Kim: any monitoring hooks we should add?
[13:17] Jordan Lee: Redwood Console can stream token-level cost, latency breakdown, and divergence/regression alerts tied to prompt sets. We'll enable the eval harness to emit alerts when delta > threshold.
[13:30] Sofia Alvarez: what logs do you need from our side?
[13:33] Priya Nair: inference traces with timestamps, prompt ids, model variant, P50/P95, and any error stacks. We also want a sample of outputs for manual review.
[13:45] Evan Brooks: we'll anonymize PII before sharing.
[13:47] Jordan Lee: perfect.
[13:50] Priya Nair: last items: we recommend starting with AWQ-4 on A100 dedicated, fall back to INT8 for critical paths if AWQ shows edge-case regressions, and keep a float16 reranker for hallucination-sensitive flows. We'll include an operational playbook for fallback routing and kernel pinning.
[14:12] Rachel Kim: that seems like a good plan. can you put the fallback routing logic in writing?
[14:17] Jordan Lee: yes — deliverable in next_steps.
[14:21] Miguel Santos: i'll also include a sample warmup script and the docker image tag to generate quant artifacts reproducibly.
[14:30] Jordan Lee: ok recap of next steps and owners. Priya will run the bench on Polaris samples; Miguel will provide warmup and docker; Arun will share VPC/firewall details; Rachel team to provision peered nodes. We'll reconvene on 2026-06-29 to review bench results.
[14:50] Rachel Kim: 6/29 works. thanks everyone.
[14:54] Jordan Lee: thanks all, meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels were inferred and there are a few transcription errors (e.g., 'KV cash' or 'GTPQ' in auto transcript) that were corrected in places but may remain.
